main.title: Zone of the Enders
main.subtitle: A machine on a damaged colony
main.summary: Zone of the Enders is Konami's PlayStation 2 mecha action game, released in Japan on 1 March 2001. A military attack leaves the young Leo Stenbuck inside Jehuty, a powerful machine called an Orbital Frame. He must deliver it to friendly forces while deciding how to respond to the people still in danger around him. The adventure puts its battles in the air, allowing Jehuty to hover, rise and move between buildings. Its mechanical design gives the player a readable, agile figure amid the destruction.

cards.heading: A machine on a damaged colony
cards.text: Zone of the Enders is Konami's PlayStation 2 mecha action game, released in Japan on 1 March 2001. A military attack leaves the young Leo Stenbuck inside Jehuty, a powerful machine called an Orbital Frame. He must deliver it to friendly forces while deciding how to respond to the people still in danger around him. The adventure puts its battles in the air, allowing Jehuty to hover, rise and move between buildings. Its mechanical design gives the player a readable, agile figure amid the destruction.

cards.heading: Close the distance
cards.text: Jehuty changes its attacks according to the distance from a target. Moving close brings the machine into blade range, while greater separation favours ranged fire. The player can dash around enemies and use a burst of power to break the rhythm of a fight. Because movement is not confined to the ground, approaching an opponent also means choosing a height and direction. Encounters move quickly between pursuit and contact, with the lock-on system keeping the selected enemy central while the surrounding colony slides past.

cards.heading: Protecting more than the pilot
cards.text: Some missions ask Leo to defend inhabited areas, making the condition of the colony part of the result. The story's civilian viewpoint gives those assignments a reason beyond destroying another formation. Noriaki Okamura directed the game, Hideo Kojima produced it, and Yoji Shinkawa designed the machines. Critics welcomed the presentation and combat but questioned the short campaign. The setting continued through other games and animation, while the direct PlayStation 2 sequel, The 2nd Runner, developed Jehuty's combat further in 2003 with a different protagonist.

main.title: Conker's Bad Fur Day
main.subtitle: Rare turns a mascot towards adult comedy
main.summary: Rare turns a familiar platforming world into a bawdy cartoon. Conker moves between film parodies, physical jokes and unexpectedly elaborate set pieces, testing how far a cheerful mascot can be pushed.

cards.heading: Rare turns a mascot towards adult comedy
cards.text: Conker's Bad Fur Day grew from Conker's Quest and Twelve Tales: Conker 64, earlier versions closer to Rare's colourful family platformers. After years of work, the team saw how crowded that territory had become. Chris Seavor proposed a more aggressive comic direction, reshaping the familiar-looking mascot around adult jokes and film parodies. The change reached the situations and rewards as well as the script, giving the Nintendo 64 game its deliberately abrasive personality.

cards.heading: An action for the occasion
cards.text: Context-sensitive actions let Conker acquire the tool needed for a particular scene. B pads and a light bulb above his head signal actions involving beer, medicine, weapons and other temporary equipment. This keeps the basic controls manageable while allowing the designers to change the rules between scenes. The setting and prompts teach the immediate task, leaving room for a succession of different jokes and challenges.

cards.heading: Film parody changes the rules
cards.text: The episodic adventure moves between platforming, chases, combat, horror scenes and war-film parody. Film references often determine how a section is framed and played, supplying objectives and changes of pace. Conker remains the link between these shifting situations, giving Rare a way to borrow from other genres within a platform adventure. Surprise comes as much from the next activity as from the next joke.

cards.heading: Voices set the comic timing
cards.text: Chris Seavor voiced numerous characters, including Conker, while Louise O'Connor performed many female roles and Robin Beanland handled sound design. Accents, pauses and vocal distortions work with animation and scene editing to establish comic timing. Having team members perform several parts helped connect those voices to the game's writing and direction, giving even brief encounters a distinctive sound.

cards.heading: Seven ways to compete locally
cards.text: Seven multiplayer variants support up to four players alongside the campaign. They reuse characters, weapons and absurd situations in short competitive scenarios with different objectives. Rare's experience with local Nintendo 64 multiplayer provides a foundation for these modes, while Conker's comic identity gives them their own tone. The same cartridge offers a sequence of directed single-player scenes and repeatable contests for people sharing a room.

cards.heading: THQ brings Conker to Europe
cards.text: THQ handled the European release on April 6, 2001, following hesitation from Nintendo of Europe. The game arrived late in the Nintendo 64's life with language-heavy adult comedy, complicating its place in the console's market. Its distribution history shows how a change in creative direction also affected the companies responsible for bringing it to players.

main.title: Castlevania: Circle of the Moon
main.subtitle: A new handheld opens another castle
main.summary: Castlevania: Circle of the Moon is Konami's Game Boy Advance action role-playing adventure following vampire hunter Nathan Graves into Dracula's castle to rescue his mentor. Released alongside the handheld in Japan, it brings the interconnected exploration associated with Symphony of the Night into a smaller screen. Fighting enemies develops Nathan's abilities while new movement options open routes through the building. Its castle is a place to learn gradually, with the discovery of another useful ability changing the meaning of a corridor or obstacle encountered earlier in the journey.

cards.heading: A new handheld opens another castle
cards.text: Castlevania: Circle of the Moon is Konami's Game Boy Advance action role-playing adventure following vampire hunter Nathan Graves into Dracula's castle to rescue his mentor. Released alongside the handheld in Japan, it brings the interconnected exploration associated with Symphony of the Night into a smaller screen. Fighting enemies develops Nathan's abilities while new movement options open routes through the building. Its castle is a place to learn gradually, with the discovery of another useful ability changing the meaning of a corridor or obstacle encountered earlier in the journey.

cards.heading: Two cards create another kind of attack
cards.text: The Dual Set-Up System combines cards associated with attributes and actions to produce magical effects. Finding a card therefore adds possibilities in relation to the collection already held, rather than supplying only one isolated ability. Different pairings can alter how Nathan attacks or responds to a difficult encounter. The system gives exploration another practical reward alongside equipment and experience. A newly discovered component may help with the immediate fight, but it can also make an older card useful in a combination that was previously unavailable to the player.

cards.heading: Return with a different way to move
cards.text: Progress through the castle depends on gaining abilities that make previously inaccessible places reachable. The map gradually becomes a record of both explored space and unfinished possibilities, encouraging the player to remember a passage that could not yet be crossed. Combat and character development support the same journey, providing the strength needed to explore further. Circle of the Moon connects those activities through its enclosed setting, making a return visit productive because Nathan may now possess a movement, an item or a card arrangement that changes what the earlier location allows.

main.title: F-Zero: Maximum Velocity
main.subtitle: A new generation of very fast machines
main.summary: F-Zero: Maximum Velocity is NDcube's Game Boy Advance racing game bringing Nintendo's high-speed series to the handheld's launch. New pilots and machines compete on tracks that rotate and scale beneath the vehicles, recalling the presentation of the original Super Nintendo game. Races demand close control near the boundaries of narrow courses, where a collision can cost more than a little speed. The portable format retains the series' emphasis on learning corners and maintaining a racing line, giving a short event enough pressure to reward repeated practice on the same route.

cards.heading: A new generation of very fast machines
cards.text: F-Zero: Maximum Velocity is NDcube's Game Boy Advance racing game bringing Nintendo's high-speed series to the handheld's launch. New pilots and machines compete on tracks that rotate and scale beneath the vehicles, recalling the presentation of the original Super Nintendo game. Races demand close control near the boundaries of narrow courses, where a collision can cost more than a little speed. The portable format retains the series' emphasis on learning corners and maintaining a racing line, giving a short event enough pressure to reward repeated practice on the same route.

cards.heading: A boost is useful only if the turn follows
cards.text: Completing a lap awards a single-use boost, providing a burst of speed at the cost of more difficult steering. Using it before a jump can extend the distance travelled, making the location of the activation as important as the immediate acceleration. Machines differ in how long their boost lasts and how they return to normal speed. The player must choose a moment that suits both the vehicle and the approaching track. A large advantage on a straight can become a problem if the next corner arrives before control has been recovered.

cards.heading: The field has a moving threshold
cards.text: Races impose position requirements as laps progress, removing a competitor who falls outside the permitted rank. The player therefore has to remain close enough to the leading field while protecting the machine from damage and avoiding falls beyond the track. Grand Prix series provide groups of races with additional difficulties and vehicles to unlock. These restrictions make survival and speed part of the same task. Finishing a course is not sufficient if the required position has already been lost, while reckless attempts to recover it can destroy the machine before the final lap.

main.title: Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil
main.subtitle: Another dream to enter
main.summary: Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil is Namco's PlayStation 2 platform adventure, first released in Japan on 21 March 2001. Klonoa arrives in the world of Lunatea and travels with the priestess-in-training Lolo and her companion Popka. Their journey crosses kingdoms associated with different emotions as a new danger approaches. The stages follow a largely fixed path through three-dimensional scenery, letting the camera turn around towers and landscapes while movement remains easy to read. Bright colours and expressive characters introduce a story that gradually becomes more melancholy.

cards.heading: Another dream to enter
cards.text: Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil is Namco's PlayStation 2 platform adventure, first released in Japan on 21 March 2001. Klonoa arrives in the world of Lunatea and travels with the priestess-in-training Lolo and her companion Popka. Their journey crosses kingdoms associated with different emotions as a new danger approaches. The stages follow a largely fixed path through three-dimensional scenery, letting the camera turn around towers and landscapes while movement remains easy to read. Bright colours and expressive characters introduce a story that gradually becomes more melancholy.

cards.heading: An enemy becomes a second jump
cards.text: Klonoa's ring captures enemies that he can carry and throw. Tossing one downward supplies an extra jump, so reaching a ledge depends on bringing the right creature to the right position. Throws can also strike switches or targets in the foreground and background. The player therefore reads enemies as moving tools as well as obstacles. Later stages combine these actions with more demanding timing, asking for a chain of captures and jumps whose solution becomes clear through the arrangement of creatures and platforms.

cards.heading: A path with room to change
cards.text: Board-riding sequences change the pace between the more deliberate platform stages and boss encounters. Collectibles and rescued inhabitants encourage another pass through a familiar Vision, while the world map provides a clear route through the adventure. Critics praised the level design and the use of three-dimensional scenery, although the game sold modestly. Hideo Yoshizawa and Yoshihiko Arawi shaped its story, supported by a large Namco music team. The original PlayStation 2 adventure later returned in the 2022 Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series compilation alongside the first game's remake.

main.title: Kuru Kuru Kururin
main.subtitle: A spinning shape needs room to pass
main.summary: Kuru Kuru Kururin is Eighting's Game Boy Advance puzzle game about guiding a constantly rotating vehicle through narrow courses. Kururin, a small bird searching for his lost siblings, pilots the long Helirin toward the goal while its ends threaten to catch the surrounding walls. The controls move the vehicle's centre, leaving its rotation as a continuing condition to anticipate. A simple-looking route becomes a question of timing and clearance, because arriving at an opening is only useful if the spinning shape can pass through it at that particular moment.

cards.heading: A spinning shape needs room to pass
cards.text: Kuru Kuru Kururin is Eighting's Game Boy Advance puzzle game about guiding a constantly rotating vehicle through narrow courses. Kururin, a small bird searching for his lost siblings, pilots the long Helirin toward the goal while its ends threaten to catch the surrounding walls. The controls move the vehicle's centre, leaving its rotation as a continuing condition to anticipate. A simple-looking route becomes a question of timing and clearance, because arriving at an opening is only useful if the spinning shape can pass through it at that particular moment.

cards.heading: Wait for the opening to fit
cards.text: The vehicle continues turning while the player moves or pauses. A narrow passage may therefore require an approach timed to the angle of the bar, followed by a movement that gives its trailing end enough room. Touching a wall causes damage, while checkpoints restore the health needed to continue. These rules make patience part of the movement system. The player can understand where to go without yet knowing how to get through, learning a route by gradually coordinating its physical space with the rhythm of the rotation.

cards.heading: A moving-day problem becomes a game
cards.text: Director Masato Toyoshima connected the idea with the experience of manoeuvring furniture while moving between apartments. The resemblance is practical: a long object must be translated and turned through spaces that were not designed around its convenience. The final game gives that everyday difficulty a bright setting and a rescue story, keeping the central relationship easy to read. Released with the Game Boy Advance in Japan, it demonstrated how a new handheld could support an engaging challenge built from one unusual shape and the space required to move it.

main.title: Game Boy Advance
main.subtitle: A wider handheld with a 32-bit processor
main.summary: Game Boy Advance widens the handheld, adds shoulder buttons and carries an existing cartridge library into a new generation.

cards.heading: A wider way to hold a game
cards.text: The original Game Boy Advance launched in Japan on 21 March 2001. Its horizontal body places the screen between the controls, with L and R buttons on the shoulders. Nintendo paired a 32-bit processor with a reflective colour display. Its model designation is AGB-001; the folding SP followed later.

cards.heading: New hardware, existing cartridges
cards.text: The cartridge slot accepted Game Boy and Game Boy Color software as well as new Advance games, subject to compatibility exceptions. Continuing an existing library gave the new machine a connection to its predecessors. New Advance cartridges were also physically smaller, making the change visible in the objects players carried.

cards.heading: Four players and a cable
cards.text: A dedicated link cable could connect up to four systems for supported software. Some games allowed multiplayer from a single cartridge; others required one in every machine. That difference mattered when arranging a game with friends. The handheld's social possibilities depended on the particular software as well as the socket on its side.

cards.heading: The landscape design and its designers
cards.text: The GBA's design featured a landscape form factor, diverging from the portrait layout of the previous Game Boy models. The design put the buttons to the sides of the device instead of below the screen. The shift was the work of French designer Gwénaël Nicolas and his Tokyo-based studio, Curiosity Inc.

cards.heading: A wider screen for richer games
cards.text: The 2.9-inch reflective display runs at 240 by 160 pixels and can show 32,000 colours. Together with the 32-bit processor, it supports richer animation, fast racing, strategy games and ambitious 2D conversions. L and R shoulder buttons expand the controls while leaving the screen between the hands. These changes give developers more room within a device still built for portable use.

main.title: Illbleed
main.subtitle: Six attractions and missing friends
main.summary: Illbleed is Crazy Games' survival horror adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 March 2001.

cards.heading: Six attractions and missing friends
cards.text: Illbleed is Crazy Games' survival horror adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 March 2001. Eriko Christy enters a horror amusement park to find her missing friends, passing through six attractions based on fictional films. Each location supplies its own story and hazards, with a deliberately lurid sense of humour connecting the park. Producer Shinya Nishigaki's team had previously made Blue Stinger under the name Climax Graphics. Here, the main problem becomes recognising the next fright before it strikes, turning the conventions of a haunted attraction into a system to learn.

cards.heading: Reading the warning signs
cards.text: A sensory display reacts to sights, sounds, smells and a sixth sense as the character approaches an item or possible trap. The Horror Monitor lets the player mark suspicious places and investigate them, spending adrenaline in the process. Correctly identifying a trap disables it and returns the spent resource. Marking an enemy can also provide an opening advantage in combat. The player therefore reads the room through both its appearance and those sensory warnings, deciding which ordinary-looking object deserves attention before another step turns suspicion into damage.

cards.heading: Fright as a physical danger
cards.text: Survival depends on stamina, heart rate and bleeding as well as the next enemy. Physical injury and sudden frights affect those measures differently, making the park dangerous in more than one way. Rescued friends become playable characters with their own strengths, while recovery items and upgrades can be purchased between expeditions. The system gives Illbleed's exaggerated horror a practical consequence: being frightened is something the character's body must withstand. Its dark comedy comes from learning to inspect an absurd spectacle carefully enough to survive the trick hidden inside it.

main.title: Animal Crossing
main.subtitle: A village that follows the calendar
main.summary: Animal Crossing, known in Japan as Dōbutsu no Mori, is a social simulation game developed and published by Nintendo.

cards.heading: A village that follows the calendar
cards.text: Nintendo's Animal Crossing, first known in Japan as Dōbutsu no Mori, makes daily life in a village follow the console's clock. Days, seasons, shop hours and villagers' routines connect play to ordinary time. Returning after an absence can reveal a changed place, while arriving for a celebration gives a real date a shared meaning with the virtual neighbours.

cards.heading: Being there at the right time
cards.text: The calendar governs when activities and encounters become available. New Year's Day makes this relationship especially visible through greetings, seasonal items and changes around the village. Players can arrive at an appointed moment or discover what happened while they were away. The same clock that organises an ordinary visit also brings exceptional days into view.

cards.heading: Midnight in the village
cards.text: New Year celebrations vary across the series. In New Horizons, Tom Nook and Isabelle host the December 31 Countdown in the plaza, with party goods and midnight fireworks. Earlier games give the occasion their own details. Returning for a particular hour creates a meeting with villagers and, in multiplayer editions, with visiting friends.

cards.heading: Objects that remember a season
cards.text: Seasonal objects connect these dates to different traditions: zodiac items, fortunes, kadomatsu and kagamimochi appear across the series. Their limited availability gives visits a purpose, while saved objects and photographs can preserve memories of earlier celebrations. A familiar event returns each year, but the collection around it records the player's own history with the village.

cards.heading: A shop closes before you arrive
cards.text: During New Leaf's development, Aya Kyogoku faced a familiar problem: coming home late could mean finding Tom Nook's shop already closed. Keeping every shop open around the clock would erase part of the difference between day and night. The team's answer connected time to the player's new position as mayor. Ordinances could adjust opening hours while preserving a town that followed ordinary time. The design addressed a particular working routine by changing the rules inside the fiction, rather than asking everyone to change the console clock.

cards.heading: Authority without a punishment meter
cards.text: The mayoral role also needed to feel present without turning the game into a demanding job. Nintendo's interview describes ceremonies added after completed projects, giving public recognition to something the player had funded. Yet the team reassures Iwata that neglected duties do not produce an approval rating or angry demands to improve. The town acknowledges participation while leaving room to decline it. A small celebration gives a completed bridge a public place in the life of the town.

cards.heading: A message waits for another player
cards.text: An earlier Nintendo seminar connects this attention to daily routines with the original Animal Crossing. Hisashi Nogami and Katsuya Eguchi discuss messages that could pass between people playing at different times. A parent arriving home late could leave something for a child to discover later. Their discussion is preserved in Matt Walker's English translation of the 2008 session. The shared village did not require simultaneous attendance to create a relationship: the same place could hold one person's action until another person was ready to encounter it.

cards.heading: Enough is different for everyone
cards.text: The seminar also challenges the assumption that a collection needs a published completion target. Eguchi and Nogami explain wanting enough objects that people could feel satisfied according to their own interests, without knowing exactly where the total ended. Furniture could give a visit purpose without making exhaustive acquisition the declared goal. Players could still pursue a complete collection, while others could stop when they had gathered the objects they wanted.

main.title: Gran Turismo 3: A-Spec
main.summary: Gran Turismo 3: A-Spec is a 2001 sim racing video game developed by Polyphony Digital and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Gran Turismo 3: A-Spec is a 2001 sim racing video game developed by Polyphony Digital and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It is the third installment in the Gran Turismo series. During its demonstration at E3 2000 and E3 2001, the game was known under the working title Gran Turismo 2000.

With previous titles being developed for the original PlayStation, Gran Turismo 3 marked the series' first foray into the sixth generation of video game consoles. Originally slated for a 2000 release as a launch title for the PlayStation 2, the game's development primarily focused on taking advantage of the console's newfound hardware capabilities. While compromising on the number of available vehicles (180, as opposed to 650 in Gran Turismo 2), the game was a significant leap forward in terms of graphics, physics, sound design, car modelling, opponent AI, environments and technical performance.

Like its predecessors, the game released to critical acclaim and was a commercial success. It went on to become the best-selling game in the series to date, the best-selling PlayStation 2 exclusive, and the second best-selling PlayStation 2 game (behind only Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas), having sold over 14.8 million copies since release. It is considered one of the greatest video games ever made. A landmark shift to the next generation of consoles, it is often cited as a turning point for the series and the sim racing genre as a whole. Its successor, Gran Turismo 4, was released in December 2004.
